db Database Plugin > Macro Usage and a Complete Example

Macro Usage and a Complete Example

db.sal is the macro facade over the native API, defining 338 macros in total. It performs the stack_alloc of out-parameter slots, the call, and the load of results for you, so SA programs do not have to write pointer arithmetic by hand. This page first explains the macros' naming and expansion rules, then gives three pieces of real end-to-end code taken from the repository's benchmark_test/, covering table creation, writes, queries, transactions, and closing. To stay faithful, the example code is quoted verbatim throughout; the .sa files in the repository themselves carry no line comments, so the numbered explanations before each code block are written in the body text.

Naming rules and list structure

  • One-to-one correspondence: DB_INIT_SCHEMA wraps sa_db_init_schema, and DB_RANGE_U64_HANDLE wraps sa_db_range_u64_handle. Converting a macro name to snake case and adding the sa_db_ prefix basically gives the native name.
  • Type-family expansion: the same shape is copied per type, for example DB_UPSERT_ROW_U64_KEY / _U32_KEY / _I32_KEY / _U8_KEY / _I8_KEY / _U16_KEY / _I16_KEY / _I64_KEY / _U64_PAIR_KEY / _U64_I64_PAIR_KEY / _BLOB_EQ_KEY; on the read side there are DB_COUNT_*_CMP_HANDLE, DB_FIND_*_HANDLE, DB_RANGE_*_HANDLE, DB_GET_*_HANDLE, DB_MIN_*_HANDLE, DB_MAX_*_HANDLE, DB_SORT_ROWS_*_HANDLE, DB_FILTER_ROWS_*_RANGE_HANDLE, and so on.
  • Read-handle suffix: _HANDLE means it acts on an already-open snapshot handle, and needs no root/table-name prefix; versions without the suffix act on the current table state.
  • Pure value-fetching macros: some macros call no native code and only load a field from an info struct, for example DB_INFO_ROW_COUNT %out_rows, %info expands to %out_rows = load %info+SaDbTableInfo_row_count as u64.

Common helper macro signatures

The parameter tables of the following five value-fetching/filling macros are taken verbatim from db.sal; the Chinese at the end of the lines is annotation added by this page:

[MACRO] DB_COLUMN_INPUT_SET %columns, %index, %data, %len
[MACRO] DB_BYTES_INPUT_SET   %inputs, %index, %data, %len
[MACRO] DB_INFO_ROW_COUNT    %out_rows, %info

[MACRO] DB_PLAN_INFO_WRITTEN          %out_written, %info
[MACRO] DB_PLAN_INFO_TOTAL            %out_total, %info
[MACRO] DB_PLAN_INFO_FIRST_PREDICATE  %out_first_predicate, %info
[MACRO] DB_PLAN_INFO_FIRST_TOTAL      %out_first_total, %info
[MACRO] DB_PLAN_INFO_SECOND_TOTAL     %out_second_total, %info
  • DB_COLUMN_INPUT_SET / DB_BYTES_INPUT_SET: at the offset %index * SIZE, write “data pointer + byte count” into a SaDbColumnInput/SaDbBytesInput array's element %index.
  • DB_INFO_ROW_COUNT: from a SaDbTableInfo, loads row_count, producing no IO at all.
  • DB_PLAN_INFO_*: read the five fields of SaDbPlanInfo.
Note[MACRO]/[END_MACRO] are the definition form inside the db.sal file; in your own .sa source you write only EXPAND … lines. Also, db.sal/schema files support // comments, but the repository's .sa example sources do not use line comments.

EXPAND syntax and internal mechanism

Macros are called through EXPAND <宏名> <实参列表>. Taking DB_INSERT_ROW as an example:

// 定义（摘自 db.sal）
[MACRO] DB_INSERT_ROW %out_status, %root, %root_len, %table_name, %table_name_len, %row, %row_len, %out_info
    %out_status = call @sa_db_insert_row(&%root, %root_len, &%table_name, %table_name_len, &%row, %row_len, &%out_info)
[END_MACRO]

// 调用（摘自 benchmark_test/db_memory_smoke.sa）
EXPAND DB_INSERT_ROW insert_a_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, row, ROW_BYTES, info

A macro that needs an out-parameter generates a temporary slot at the expansion site and reads it back, for example DB_SUM_U64_HANDLE:

[MACRO] DB_SUM_U64_HANDLE %out_status, %out_sum, %handle, %column_index
    __db_handle_sum_slot_%out_sum = stack_alloc 8
    ...call...(&__db_handle_sum_slot_%out_sum)
    %out_sum = load __db_handle_sum_slot_%out_sum+0 as u64
[END_MACRO]
NoteThe slot name is formed from the out-parameter variable name, so expanding the same macro multiple times on different out-parameters does not conflict; but do not use identifiers that would produce a same-name conflict as out-parameters. Every status code should be compared against SA_DB_OK before continuing.

String constants and lengths

Parameters such as root, table name, and schema text are all passed as a “pointer + byte length” pair. Real examples uniformly declare them like this:

@import "db.sal"

@const ROOT = utf8:"."
@const TABLE = utf8:"blob_key_write_smoke"
@const SCHEMA_PATH = utf8:"blob_key_write_smoke.sadb-schema"
@const SCHEMA = utf8:"#def MAX_ROWS = 8\n#def COL_ID_STRIDE = 8 // u64\n#def COL_CODE_STRIDE = 8 // blob_handle\n#def COL_POINTS_STRIDE = 8 // u64\n"

#def ROOT_LEN = 1
#def TABLE_LEN = 20
#def SCHEMA_PATH_LEN = 32
#def SCHEMA_LEN = 122
#def ROW_BYTES = 24

A *_LEN must equal the exact byte count (UTF-8) of the corresponding string; getting it wrong leads to out-of-bounds reads or match failures. Note that the // u64 in the schema text is the schema's type annotation, not an .sa comment.

Example one: a complete lifecycle on an in-memory root

Source: benchmark_test/db_memory_smoke.sa. It demonstrates the correct order the README stresses — build indexes before the first write — and the four main paths of tx, coltx, read handles, and verify. All the key steps are kept below, omitting the item-by-item assertion chain and the ownership-release block at the end.

Declaration area: the in-memory root :memory:sa_smoke, a two-column u64 table, row width 16 bytes:

@import "db.sal"

@const ROOT = utf8:":memory:sa_smoke"
@const TABLE = utf8:"mem_sa_members"
@const SCHEMA_PATH = utf8:"mem_sa_members.sadb-schema"
@const SCHEMA = utf8:"#def MAX_ROWS = 8\n#def COL_ID_STRIDE = 8 // u64\n#def COL_POINTS_STRIDE = 8 // u64\n"

#def ROOT_LEN = 16
#def TABLE_LEN = 14
#def SCHEMA_PATH_LEN = 26
#def SCHEMA_LEN = 82
#def ROW_BYTES = 16
#def COL_BYTES = 8
#def COLUMN_COUNT = 2
#def COLUMNS_BYTES = 32

@main() -> i32:
L_ENTRY:
    info = stack_alloc SaDbTableInfo_SIZE
    snapshot_info = stack_alloc SaDbSnapshotInfo_SIZE
    columns = stack_alloc COLUMNS_BYTES
    ids_col = alloc COL_BYTES
    points_col = alloc COL_BYTES
    row = alloc ROW_BYTES

Step one, idempotent cleanup + initialize the schema + build a unique index before the first write:

    EXPAND DB_REMOVE_TABLE remove_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, info
    EXPAND DB_INIT_SCHEMA init_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, SCHEMA_PATH, SCHEMA_PATH_LEN, SCHEMA, SCHEMA_LEN, info
    EXPAND DB_CREATE_U64_INDEX create_index_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, 0, 1, info

Step two, a single-table transaction: insert two rows and commit once, after which reading back the row count should give 2:

    EXPAND DB_TX_BEGIN tx_begin_status, tx, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN
    store row+0, 1 as u64
    store row+8, 10 as u64
    EXPAND DB_TX_INSERT_ROW tx_insert1_status, tx, row, ROW_BYTES, info
    store row+0, 2 as u64
    store row+8, 20 as u64
    EXPAND DB_TX_INSERT_ROW tx_insert2_status, tx, row, ROW_BYTES, info
    EXPAND DB_TX_COMMIT tx_commit_status, tx, info
    EXPAND DB_INFO_ROW_COUNT tx_rows, info

Step three, a coltx column batch session: assemble a batch of data by column (here 1 row, 2 columns); after committing, the total row count is 3. Note that DB_COLUMN_INPUT_SET fills the column descriptor array as (数组, 列序号, 数据指针, 字节数):

    EXPAND DB_COLTX_BEGIN coltx_begin_status, coltx, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN
    store ids_col+0, 3 as u64
    store points_col+0, 30 as u64
    EXPAND DB_COLUMN_INPUT_SET columns, 0, ids_col, COL_BYTES
    EXPAND DB_COLUMN_INPUT_SET columns, 1, points_col, COL_BYTES
    EXPAND DB_COLTX_ADD_COLUMNS coltx_add_status, coltx, 1, columns, COLUMN_COUNT
    EXPAND DB_COLTX_COMMIT coltx_commit_status, coltx, info
    EXPAND DB_INFO_ROW_COUNT coltx_rows, info

Step four, open a read handle and query: sum_points should be 60, found_id3 being 1 means it was found and the row number is 1, and points_id3 is 30:

    EXPAND DB_OPEN_READ_TABLE open_status, read_handle, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN
    EXPAND DB_SNAPSHOT_INFO_HANDLE shape_status, read_handle, snapshot_info
    EXPAND DB_SNAPSHOT_INFO_ROW_COUNT shape_rows, snapshot_info
    EXPAND DB_SUM_U64_HANDLE sum_status, sum_points, read_handle, 1
    EXPAND DB_FIND_U64_HANDLE find_status, found_id3, row_id3, read_handle, 0, 3
    EXPAND DB_GET_U64_HANDLE get_status, points_id3, read_handle, 1, row_id3
    EXPAND DB_CLOSE_READ_TABLE close_status, read_handle
    EXPAND DB_VERIFY verify_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, info

Step five, wrap up: the source file eqs each step's status code against its expected value into a boolean one by one, chains them with and into a single master switch, and finally releases ownership uniformly:

    ok_init = eq init_status, SA_DB_OK
    ok_sum = eq sum_points, 60
    ok01 = and ok_init, ok_sum
    ok = and ok01, ok_verify

    !remove_status
    !init_status
    !row
    !ids_col
    !points_col
    br ok -> L_OK, L_FAIL

L_OK:
    !ok
    return 0

L_FAIL:
    !ok
    panic(9003)
NoteThe wrap-up block above is a version simplified for explanation; the real file's assertion chain has more than twenty items, and its release list is much more complete. Both the L_OK and L_FAIL labels must each release ok; this is the standard way to avoid leaks under flat control flow.

Example two: writing and reading with a blob business key

Source: benchmark_test/db_blob_key_write_smoke.sa. The table structure is id:u64 + code:blob_handle + points:u64, using a blob exact value as the business key.

Prepare the blob store: append customer codes to the named store codes, returning stable 1-based handles, the first returning 1, the second 2, and so on:

    EXPAND DB_BLOB_PUT put_a_status, code_a_id, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN,
                       STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_A, CODE_LEN, info
    EXPAND DB_BLOB_PUT put_b_status, code_b_id, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN,
                       STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_B, CODE_LEN, info
    EXPAND DB_BLOB_PUT put_c_status, code_c_id, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN,
                       STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_C, CODE_LEN, info

Assemble a 24-byte row and insert it, then build a blob_eq index with unique=1 — without this index there is no key-based write path that follows:

    store row+0, 1 as u64
    store row+8, code_a_id as u64
    store row+16, 100 as u64
    EXPAND DB_INSERT_ROW insert_a_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, row, ROW_BYTES, info

    store row+0, 2 as u64
    store row+8, code_b_id as u64
    store row+16, 200 as u64
    EXPAND DB_INSERT_ROW insert_b_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, row, ROW_BYTES, info

    EXPAND DB_CREATE_BLOB_EQ_INDEX index_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, 1, STORE, STORE_LEN, 1, info

Strict update and upsert. Note the parameter order: first two 1s (the unique flag and the fixed argument in the column-number position, respectively), then the store name and the key value:

    store row+0, 2 as u64
    store row+8, code_b_id as u64
    store row+16, 250 as u64
    EXPAND DB_UPDATE_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY direct_update_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, 1,
            STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_B, CODE_LEN, row, ROW_BYTES, info

    store row+0, 2 as u64
    store row+8, code_b_id as u64
    store row+16, 260 as u64
    EXPAND DB_UPSERT_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY direct_upsert_existing_status, direct_upsert_existing_inserted,
            ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, 1, STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_B, CODE_LEN, row, ROW_BYTES, info

Mixed operations inside a transaction, then commit: inside the transaction, append a new blob, upsert a new row, and delete an old row, taking effect in one commit. A control group opens a second transaction, does the same thing, and then rolls back, so none of the changes take effect: 

    EXPAND DB_TX_BEGIN tx_begin_status, tx, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN
    EXPAND DB_TX_BLOB_PUT tx_blob_d_status, code_d_id, tx, STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_D, CODE_LEN, info
    store row+0, 4 as u64
    store row+8, code_d_id as u64
    store row+16, 400 as u64
    EXPAND DB_TX_UPSERT_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY tx_upsert_new_status, tx_upsert_new_inserted, tx, 1,
            STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_D, CODE_LEN, row, ROW_BYTES, info
    EXPAND DB_TX_DELETE_BLOB_EQ_KEY tx_delete_status, tx, 1, STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_B, CODE_LEN, info
    EXPAND DB_TX_COMMIT tx_commit_status, tx, info
    EXPAND DB_INFO_ROW_COUNT rows_after_commit, info

    EXPAND DB_TX_BEGIN tx2_begin_status, tx2, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN
    EXPAND DB_TX_BLOB_PUT tx2_blob_f_status, code_f_id, tx2, STORE, STORE_LEN, CODE_F, CODE_LEN, info
    EXPAND DB_TX_ROLLBACK tx2_rollback_status, tx2

Fetch a whole row directly by unique blob key on a read handle, and verify at the end:

    EXPAND DB_OPEN_READ_TABLE open_status, read_handle, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN
    EXPAND DB_GET_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY_HANDLE get_c_status, read_handle, 1, STORE, STORE_LEN,
            CODE_C, CODE_LEN, fetched_row, ROW_BYTES
    fetched_c_id = load fetched_row+0 as u64
    fetched_c_code = load fetched_row+8 as u64
    fetched_c_points = load fetched_row+16 as u64
    EXPAND DB_CLOSE_READ_TABLE close_status, read_handle
    EXPAND DB_VERIFY verify_status, ROOT, ROOT_LEN, TABLE, TABLE_LEN, info

This program also verifies the expected return values of three kinds of failure paths, and can be used directly as a behavioral reference:

OperationScenarioExpected return
DB_UPDATE_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEYKey existsSA_DB_OK
DB_UPDATE_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEYKey missingSA_DB_ERR_NOT_FOUND, does not append
DB_UPDATE_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEYThe row's blob_handle bytes differ from the key parameterSA_DB_ERR_INVALID_FORMAT
DB_UPSERT_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY's out_insertedAn existing key0
DB_UPSERT_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY's out_insertedA new key1
DB_DELETE_BLOB_EQ_KEYDeleting an already-deleted key againSA_DB_ERR_NOT_FOUND
DB_GET_ROW_BLOB_EQ_KEY_HANDLEA key that was rolled backSA_DB_ERR_NOT_FOUND

Example three: a planner two-predicate query

Source: benchmark_test/db_planner_smoke.sa. The table structure carries logical annotations: #def COL_STATUS_STRIDE = 8 // u64, #def COL_DUE_DAY_STRIDE = 8 // i64 date, #def COL_AMOUNT_CENTS_STRIDE = 8 // i64 decimal(2). The planner estimates the candidate size of each of the two predicates and scans the smaller side first:

    plan_info = stack_alloc SaDbPlanInfo_SIZE
    plan_rows = alloc ROWS_BYTES

    EXPAND DB_PLAN_U64_I64_RANGES_HANDLE tie_plan_status, plan_rows, ROWS_CAP, plan_info,
            read_handle, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1500, 5500, 0, ROWS_CAP

    EXPAND DB_PLAN_INFO_WRITTEN tie_written, plan_info
    EXPAND DB_PLAN_INFO_TOTAL tie_total, plan_info
    EXPAND DB_PLAN_INFO_FIRST_PREDICATE tie_first_predicate, plan_info
    EXPAND DB_PLAN_INFO_FIRST_TOTAL tie_first_total, plan_info
    EXPAND DB_PLAN_INFO_SECOND_TOTAL tie_second_total, plan_info

    EXPAND DB_PLAN_U64_I64_RANGES_HANDLE page_plan_status, plan_rows, ROWS_CAP, plan_info,
            read_handle, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1500, 5500, 1, 1

The first call is a full match (offset=0, limit=ROWS_CAP), and the second turns only one page (offset=1, limit=1), to verify the paging contract. The predicate order is “u64 range (column 1: 2..2) + i64 range (column 3: 1500..5500)”; first_predicate returning 1 or 2 indicates which side the planner actually scanned first, with ties taking 1.

WarningWhat is passed to range/planner is the already-encoded integer value: a date must first be converted to epoch days with DB_DATE_FROM_YMD, an amount must first be converted with DB_DECIMAL_FROM_PARTS to a scaled integer, and a timestamp must use DB_TIMESTAMP_MS_FROM_PARTS/DB_TIMESTAMP_US_FROM_PARTS. i64 date / decimal(2) are only metadata annotations; the physical bytes are still an ordinary i64.

Self-check list

  1. Is @import "db.sal" at the very top? The macros and constants (including SA_DB_OK) all come from it.
  2. Does every string constant have a paired *_LEN with the correct byte count?
  3. Before a unique-key write path, has a unique index of the corresponding type already been built?
  4. For bulk concurrent imports, did you use coltx rather than bare ingest_columns?
  5. Has every out-parameter's status code been checked? Are failures concentrated at a single failure label?
  6. After using a read handle, is there a DB_CLOSE_READ_TABLE? Does the wrap-up run DB_VERIFY?
  7. Does every intermediate value have a corresponding ! release? This is a general SA discipline, not a db-plugin-specific requirement.

For the native semantics behind each macro, see The Eight SA API Groups; for the equivalent operations on the command-line side, see CLI Commands in Detail; for performance and limits, see Limits, Performance, and Best Practices.
